courses.title: Introduction to Criminology
courses.description: Introduction to criminology. Systematic analysis of the history, theories and major works of the field. Contemporary issues and debates.

courses.title: Research Methods in Criminology
courses.description: Examines how research is conducted in criminology and criminal justice. Designed to highlight the research process, ethical issues, and different types of quantitative and qualitative research designs, data analysis, and the evaluation and reporting of research results in the field of criminology. The following methods of criminological research are explored: ethnography, ethnomethodology, conversation analysis, narrative analysis, comparative analyses, case studies, evaluation research, and elementary statistical analysis and survey design.

courses.title: Research Methods in Sociology
courses.description: Introduction and intermediate exposure to the following methods of sociological research: ethnography, interviews, discourse and content analysis, focus groups, and elementary statistical analysis and survey design.

courses.title: Research Methods in Psychology
courses.description: Introduction and intermediate exposure to the methods, techniques, and data analysis used in carrying out research in psychology.
courses.prerequisites: Major or minor in PSY; PSY 2201 , PSY 201, or PSY 202; STA 1200 , STA 1202 , or STA 120; and GE Area 1A/A2.

courses.title: Crime Analysis
courses.description: Introduction to intelligence analysis and its application in law enforcement. Corequisite(s): CRM 3306A .
courses.prerequisites: CRM 2201 , CRM 2205 or SOC 2205 , and senior standing.

courses.title: Crime Analysis Activity
courses.description: Introduction to intelligence analysis and its application in law enforcement. Corequisite(s): CRM 3306 .
courses.prerequisites: CRM 2201 , SOC 2205 or CRM 2205 , and senior standing.

courses.title: Criminological Theory
courses.description: Explores both historical and contemporary theories of the causes of crime. In addition to understanding the basic theoretical foundation of criminological theory, placement of those theories within their particular historical and political contexts. Examination of contemporary theories of crime.

courses.title: Senior Symposium
courses.description: Contemporary concepts, issues, and studies in criminology. Seminar-discussions. Writing-Intensive courses must be passed with a C or higher to count towards the University’s 3-unit Writing Requirement.
courses.prerequisites: SOC 2201 or CRM 2201 , and junior or senior standing.
courses.repeat_for_credit: May be taken multiple times only with different topics Minimum - Maximum Units: Total credit limited to 6 units, with a maximum of 3 units per semester.

courses.title: Introduction to Sociology
courses.description: [GE 4A] Introduction to the study and practice of sociology. Key theories, ideas, concepts and principles. Theories, methods and key areas of study such as culture, socialization, globalization, gender/sexuality, race/ethnicity. Must be taken for a letter grade by Sociology majors.

courses.title: Crime, Criminalization and Society
courses.description: [GE 4C] Introduction to a social science understandings of crime. Topics covered include: criminalization of youth, drug policy, policing, internet crime, and the underground economy.
courses.prerequisites: Junior or senior standing; and completion of GE Areas 1 and 2, or Areas A and B4 are recommended.

courses.title: Qualitative Methods for Sociology
courses.description: Advanced qualitative methods in sociology. Conduct a semester long qualitative research project using ethnographic field methods and in-depth interviewing. Students will be required to conduct at least 5 hours of qualitative data collection each week and collect 100-150 single spaced pages of field notes and interview transcripts. Writing-Intensive courses must be passed with a C or higher to count towards the University’s 3-unit Writing Requirement. Corequisite(s): SOC 4110L .
courses.prerequisites: SOC 2201 or CRM 2201 , SOC 2205 or CRM 2205 , and junior or senior standing.

courses.title: Qualitative Methods for Sociology Laboratory
courses.description: Advanced qualitative methods in sociology. In this class, students will conduct a semester long qualitative research project using ethnographic field methods and in-depth interviewing. Students will be required to conduct at least 5 hours of qualitative data collection each week and collect 100-150 single spaced pages of field notes and interview transcripts. Corequisite(s): SOC 4110W .
courses.prerequisites: SOC 201, SOC 2201 , or CRM 2201 ; and SOC 2205 , SOC 204, or CRM 2205 .

courses.title: Statistics with Applications
courses.description: [GE 2] Sample and population data; descriptive statistics, including numerical and graphical summarization of central tendency and spread; elementary probability, including events, basic probability rules, binomial and normal distributions; inferential statistics, including confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for one-population mean and proportion problems, simple linear regression and correlation
courses.prerequisites: Category I, Category II, ALEKS >=46, C or better in a GE Sub-area 2/B4 course, or C- or better or CR in MAT 1051 .

courses.title: Forensic Anthropology
courses.description: [GE 5D] Theory and techniques of forensic science. Instruction in human anatomy, osteology, and dentition; tools of anthropometry, facial reconstruction. Visiting experts in field applications (autopsies, crime scene analysis, criminal profiling, mortuary practices). Analysis in paleodemography, epidemiology.
courses.prerequisites: Junior or senior standing; and completion of GE Areas 1 and 2, or Areas A and B4 are recommended.

courses.title: White Collar Crime
courses.description: Defining, measuring and understanding the scale of white collar crime along with the major theoretical influences on its study.

courses.title: Criminal Law and the Courts
courses.description: Examines criminal cases after arrest but before the sentence is imposed. Outlines the evolving roles of the judge, prosecutor, and defense attorney. Discusses major challenges and controversies during bail, arraignment, trial, and sentencing, including cash bail and pre-trial detention, plea bargaining, jury selection, sentencing outcomes, like incarceration, and disparities.

courses.title: Policing
courses.description: History and organization of police in the United States. Police organizations, controversies and reforms are covered.

courses.title: Probation and Parole
courses.description: Theoretical and philosophical basis of probation and parole. Historical background; development and practice of investigation; supervision and treatment role of probation and parole officers. Past and present treatment models related to officer, offender, and community.

courses.title: Mass Incarceration
courses.description: [GE 4C] Drawing upon theoretical and empirical insights from sociology, criminology, law, and other fields, this course explores the causes and consequences of mass incarceration in the United States. Specifically, the course will examine the historical foundations of mass incarceration; how sentencing policy, policing, and prosecution have oiled the engine of mass imprisonment; what correctional practices look like in the everyday; the consequences of mass incarceration for those incarcerated, their families, and their respective communities; and the implications of incarceration for mobility, inequality, and equity in the U.S. The course will also explore how other countries practice incarceration in order to identify alternative approaches and place American policy and practice in global perspective.
courses.prerequisites: Junior or senior standing; and completion of GE Areas 1 and 2, or Areas A and B4 are recommended.

courses.title: Restorative Justice
courses.description: Introduction and application of restorative justice in history and practice. Current issues related to restorative justice and nonviolent approaches to justice.

courses.title: Juvenile Delinquency
courses.description: Juvenile delinquency in California and elsewhere; types and extent; theories of causation; laws, courts, correctional institutions, probation; new programs.

courses.title: Drug Policy
courses.description: History of American drug policy, a sociological examination of the war on drugs, globalization of the drug trade, future directions in drug policy.

courses.title: Political Violence
courses.description: Examination of the configuration and organization of historical and contemporary political violence from an international and global perspective. Comparison of different forms of political violence and comparison of forms of counterinsurgency and counterterrorism. Critical discussion of the theoretical views of political violence, peacemaking, and nonviolence.

courses.title: Media and Crime
courses.description: [GE 4C] Exploration of the complicated relationship between media and crime. Theoretical insights from media studies, sociology, cultural studies, ethnic and area studies, and criminology will be used to problematize this relationship. How media impacts priorities for law enforcement, funding and discourse on crime. How media depictions of crime impact politics, popular culture, economics, and social policy.
courses.prerequisites: Junior or senior standing; and completion of GE Areas 1 and 2, or Areas A and B4 are recommended.

courses.title: Race and Ethnic Relations
courses.description: Focuses on race and ethnic relations in the U.S. Examines historical and contemporary issues of racism and experiences of ethnic minorities in the U.S. Examines the future of race and ethnic relations and emphasizes current ethnic contacts, conflicts, and coalitions.

courses.title: Community and Urban Sociology
courses.description: Examination of the configuration and organization of the city through urban theories and research. A historical orientation is also undertaken to illuminate social dynamic patterns such as community and cultural relations that have shaped modern urban life. Analyses of ongoing trends in urban and suburban communities will also be undertaken.

courses.title: Gender and Sexuality
courses.description: Interrogates how gender and sexuality exist as organizing principles of society in political, economic, cultural and familial contexts within selected western and non-western societies. A critical focus on the intersection of gender and sexuality across class, racial-ethnic groups, cultures, and regions.

courses.title: Immigration and Migration
courses.description: Historical and contemporary eras of immigration to the United States. Comparison of the migration and acculturation experiences of different national origin groups from Europe, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Africa to deepen our understanding of frameworks related to push/pull factors, assimilation, and incorporation.

courses.title: Demography and Public Policy
courses.description: How populations change across time in terms of size, distribution, and key characteristics. How these factors influence public policy is central. How policies change across time, and their impact on the populations is covered.

courses.title: Family Violence
courses.description: Critically examines causes and consequences of various forms of family violence such as child abuse, intimate partner abuse, and elder abuse. Includes theory, research interventions, and services at the local, national and international level that attempt both to address and prevent family violence.

courses.title: Internship
courses.description: An internship course open to SW option students, SOC majors and CRM majors. Students must secure an internship before enrolling in the course. Internship information located on the sociology department website.
courses.prerequisites: SOC 2201 , SW 2201 , or CRM 2201 ; and SOC 4401 or SW 4990 .
courses.repeat_for_credit: May be taken multiple times Minimum - Maximum Units: Total credit limited to 6 units, with a maximum of 3 units per semester.

courses.title: Human Rights
courses.description: Introduction to the study of human rights in a global context. It will prepare students to critically engage with the dominant theoretical discussions and discourses within the field as well as analyze the complex human rights abuses and frameworks for action.

courses.title: Special Topics for Upper Division Students
courses.description: Group study at an advanced level of a selected well-defined topic or area not covered by a regularly offered course.
courses.repeat_for_credit: May be taken multiple times only with different topics Minimum - Maximum Units: Total credit limited to 6 units applicable to a degree, with a maximum of 2 sections per semester.

courses.title: Cal Poly Pomona Undergraduate Sponsored Summer Experience
courses.description: Enrollment in this 0-unit course allows students to receive university services while participating in a Cal Poly Pomona sponsored summer experience.
